--- title: "Notebook 2 — A silicon audience: writing ads for five kinds of voter" subtitle: LLMSS 2026, Workshop 3 (The Silicon Audience), Silicon Voters block · Hong Kong, 13 October 2026 output: html_document: toc: true toc_float: true df_print: kable --- ## What you will do A **silicon audience** is a panel of digital twins: a language model, given one voter's record, predicts how that voter would answer a question about a political message. The Talking to Machines group uses such panels to decide which message reaches which voter *before* the message runs, and it is testing the panels against the people they are built from in a pre-registered study (OSF, 7 October 2026). In this notebook a language model writes a thirty-second television ad, and you improve the instructions it is given, in three stages. Every ad is aimed at one of five kinds of Ohio voter, from strong Democrats to strong Republicans, and every ad gets two scores: - **Does it read like a real ad?** Judges compare it with a real Ohio campaign ad and try to spot the machine-written one. - **Does it hit its group?** The twins say how likely they would be to vote for the candidate behind it, and the ad should do better with its own group than with the other four. The sections, in about forty-five minutes: 1. **The Voters:** the 400 Ohio twins you built this morning, in five groups; 2. **The question:** your issue, and the one question every twin answers; 3. **The study's scripts:** how the five groups rated the scripts in the pre-registered study, and how to read a score that is about *aim*; 4. **Stage 1:** a basic prompt writes five ads, one per group; 5. **Stage 2:** the same prompt with what our tests taught us added; 6. **Stage 3:** your prompt, run live: push the aim higher than Stage 2; 7. **The leaderboard,** and what the loop does next; 8. **What a twin cannot know.** Stages 1 and 2, and one worked example of Stage 3, were run once by the organisers and ship with the notebook, so the same prompt gives everyone the same ads and the same scores. Only Stage 3 calls a language model, and only if an API key is set. Everything else runs offline from the files beside this notebook. **How to read this notebook.** As in the morning's notebooks, every table, text block and figure the code prints has a number, given in bold just above the code that prints it, and the text says which table, row or column a number comes from. **Figure 0.1.** The loop. The optimiser runs the ring over hundreds of messages; this notebook walks it by hand, three times, with the audience and the question already built. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](../figures/loop_map.png){width=100%} ::: ::: The first block loads the packages the notebook uses and sets the folders it reads from and writes to. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(data.table) library(jsonlite) library(ggplot2) DATA <- file.path("..", "data") OUT <- file.path("..", "output") dir.create(OUT, showWarnings = FALSE) read_parquet <- function(f) { # arrow on the workshop server; nanoparquet is a light fallback if (requireNamespace("arrow", quietly = TRUE)) as.data.table(arrow::read_parquet(f)) else as.data.table(nanoparquet::read_parquet(f)) } GROUPS <- data.table( group = c("SD", "WD", "IND", "WR", "SR"), label = c("Strong Democrat", "Weak or leaning Democrat", "Independent", "Weak or leaning Republican", "Strong Republican"), phrase = c("strong Democrats", "weak or leaning Democrats", "independents", "weak or leaning Republicans", "strong Republicans")) GROUP_COLOURS <- c(SD = "#1f4e9c", WD = "#7fa6dd", IND = "#8c8c8c", WR = "#e39a8f", SR = "#b0281a") ``` ::: --- ## 1. The Voters The audience is the 400-twin Ohio panel from Workshop 1: a seeded draw from the census frame, each twin matched to a Cooperative Election Study respondent and rendered as a persona. The panel ships with this notebook as a copy, so you do not need the morning's `output/` folder, but it is the same 400 twins with the same personas, character for character. Every persona carries the matched respondent's own **party identification** on the seven-point scale. The block below reads it from the persona and puts each twin in one of five groups: strong Democrats; weak or leaning Democrats; independents; weak or leaning Republicans; strong Republicans. A twin whose respondent answered "not sure" is in none of the five and is left out of the group tables. **Table 1.1.** `panel`: the 400 twins, by party identification and the group it puts them in. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} panel <- read_parquet(file.path(DATA, "oh_panel_400.parquet")) panel[, pid7 := sub("^- Party identification: ", "", regmatches(persona_text, regexpr("- Party identification: [^\n]+", persona_text)))] PID_TO_GROUP <- c("Strong Democrat" = "SD", "Not Very Strong Democrat" = "WD", "Lean Democrat" = "WD", "Independent" = "IND", "Lean Republican" = "WR", "Not Very Strong Republican" = "WR", "Strong Republican" = "SR") panel[, group := unname(PID_TO_GROUP[pid7])] panel[, .N, by = .(pid7, group)][order(match(group, GROUPS$group))] ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|pid7 |group | N| |:--------------------------|:-----|--:| |Strong Democrat |SD | 90| |Lean Democrat |WD | 37| |Not Very Strong Democrat |WD | 31| |Independent |IND | 38| |Lean Republican |WR | 49| |Not Very Strong Republican |WR | 45| |Strong Republican |SR | 94| |Not Sure |NA | 16|
::: ::: The next block prints one persona in full: this is everything the twin is told about who it is, exactly as the morning's model read it. Change `TWIN` to read another. Notice the provenance line at the head of each section — modelled from the census cell, or the matched respondent's own answer — and notice what is *not* there: no advertisement, no rating of one, nothing about this study. **Text 1.1.** The persona of twin `TWIN`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} TWIN <- panel$twin_id[1] cat(panel[twin_id == TWIN, persona_text]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` === PROFILE === The following is a record describing an adult citizen in the state of Ohio. It describes who you are: your civic record, your circumstances, your values and your political opinions. Each section states where the information comes from. -- CIVIC RECORD (not observed: synthetic skeleton drawn from the census frame, no voter-file record) -- - Congressional district: OH-01 - Voted in the November 2024 general election: yes (modelled from the census frame) - Earlier general elections, primary participation, registration: (not observed) -- DEMOGRAPHICS (census frame cell; modelled fields marked, respondent's own answers marked) -- - Age: 35 - Sex: Female (census frame cell; modelled) - Ethnicity: Middle Eastern (the matched survey respondent's own answer) - Education: Postgraduate degree (the matched survey respondent's own answer) - Household income: Prefer not to say (the matched survey respondent's own answer, CES 2025) - Marital status: Married (the matched survey respondent's own answer) -- VALUES & POLITICS (donated from CES 2025 respondent #2524025786) -- - Party identification: Lean Democrat - Party identification including leaners: Democrat (Including Leaners) - Ideology: Liberal - Retrospective economic evaluation (as of 2025): Gotten much worse - Presidential approval (as of 2025): Strongly Disapprove - Issue positions (the donor's own answers, CES 2025): - Ukraine (as of 2025): Impose economic sanctions on Russia; Send food, medicine, and other humanitarian aid to Ukraine - Israel/Gaza (as of 2025): Send food, medicine and other aid to the communities affected - Gun control - Ban assault rifles: Support - Gun control - Make it easier for people to obtain concealed-carry permit: Oppose - Gun control - Require criminal background checks on all gun sales: Support - Gun control - Increase the number of police on the street by 10 percent, even if it means fewer funds for other public services: Oppose - Gun control - Decrease the number of police on the street by 10 percent, and increase funding for other public services: Support - Grant legal status to all illegal immigrants who have held jobs and paid taxes for at least 3 years, and not been convicted of any felony crimes: Support - Increase the number of border patrols on the US-Mexican border: Oppose - Build a wall between the U.S. and Mexico: Oppose - Provide permanent resident status to children of immigrants who were brought to the United States by their parents (also known as Dreamers). Provide these immigrants a pathway to citizenship if they meet the citizenship requirements and have committed no crimes: Support - Give the Environmental Protection Agency power to regulate carbon dioxide emissions: Support - Require that at least 20 percent of electricity be generated with renewable sources such as wind, solar, or hydroelectric power: Support - Strengthen the Environmental Protection Agency enforcement of the Clean Air Act and Clean Water Act even if it costs U.S. jobs: Support - Increase fossil fuel production in the U.S: Oppose - Halt new oil and gas leases on federal lands: Support - Relax local zoning laws in your state to allow for construction of more apartments and condos: Oppose - Expand federal tax incentives to encourage developers to build homes for people who make less than half of the average income in your area: Support - Require able-bodied adults under 64 years of age who do not have dependents to have a job in order to receive Medicaid: Support - Repeal the Affordable Care Act: Oppose -- CIRCUMSTANCES & BELIEFS (donated from CES 2025 respondent #2524025786; the respondent's own answers) -- - Employment status: Part-time - Home: Own - Children under 18 in the household: Yes - Number of children: not asked in this respondent's survey (CES 2025) - Parent or guardian of: a child under 18 - Household income change over the past year (as of 2025): Stayed about the same - Prices of everyday goods over the past year (as of 2025): Increased a lot - If faced with an unexpected $400 expense: not asked in this respondent's survey (CES 2025) - Labour union member: I formerly was a member of a labor union - Union member elsewhere in the household: A member of my household was formerly a member of a labor union, but is not now - Covered by a union contract: No - Religion: Something else - Born-again or evangelical Christian: No - Importance of religion: Not at all important - Attends religious services: Never - Prays: Never - Views on race and gender: not asked in this respondent's survey (CES 2025) -- MEDIA DIET (donated from CES 2025 respondent #2524025786) -- - Interest in news and public affairs: Only now and then - Media market (DMA): (absent) - Media use in the past 24 hours (the donor's own answers, as of 2025): - Used: TV news, a newspaper (print or online) - Did not use: social media, radio news - Type of TV news watched: national news - TV networks watched: ABC - Type of newspaper read: online - Political activity on social media: not applicable (did not use social media) === END OF PROFILE === ``` ::: ::: --- ## 2. The question Pick one of the two issues in Table 2.1 and put it in `ISSUE`. Every ad you see from here on is about that issue. **Table 2.1.** `issues`: the two issues in this block. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} issues <- fread(file.path(DATA, "issues.csv"))[key %in% c("COST", "IMM")] ISSUE <- "immigration" # or "taxes and household relief" it <- issues[issue == ISSUE] issues[, .(key, issue, title)] ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|key |issue |title | |:----|:--------------------------|:--------------------------| |COST |taxes and household relief |Taxes and household relief | |IMM |immigration |Immigration |
::: ::: Every ad is put to every twin with **one question**: how likely this person would be to vote for the candidate behind the ad, from 0 (certainly not) to 10 (certainly would). It is the vote-likelihood item of the pre-registered study, word for word. The **header** tells the model what it is doing: *predicting* the answer a particular person would give, in the third person ("this person"), from that person's record. That is how the registered study puts it, and it is not the same as asking the model to *be* the person. The **profile** is the persona you read in Text 1.1; then comes the ad, and the question. The twin is never told which group an ad was written for, who wrote it, or what the study is about. The block below defines the header, the question and the JSON schema the answer must match, and prints them. **Text 2.1.** The question, as sent (the profile omitted). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} HEADER <- paste( "Below is the profile of an adult in Ohio, and then a political advertisement. Predict how this", "person would answer the question that follows: give the answer this person would actually give,", "not the answer a typical person would give, and not the one you would wish them to give.", "Return only the JSON object described at the end.") question_block <- function(script) paste0( "Here is the script for a thirty-second television advertisement by a candidate running for office.\n\n", script, "\n\n", "After reading this, how likely would this person be to vote for the candidate behind this advertisement?\n", "0 = certainly not, 10 = certainly would.\n", "Return: {\"ptv\": <0-10>}") SCHEMA <- list(type = "object", additionalProperties = FALSE, required = list("ptv"), properties = list(ptv = list(type = "integer", minimum = 0, maximum = 10))) cat(HEADER, "\n\n=== PROFILE ===\n{persona_text}\n=== END OF PROFILE ===\n\n", sep = "") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Below is the profile of an adult in Ohio, and then a political advertisement. Predict how this person would answer the question that follows: give the answer this person would actually give, not the answer a typical person would give, and not the one you would wish them to give. Return only the JSON object described at the end. === PROFILE === {persona_text} === END OF PROFILE === ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat(question_block("{script}")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Here is the script for a thirty-second television advertisement by a candidate running for office. {script} After reading this, how likely would this person be to vote for the candidate behind this advertisement? 0 = certainly not, 10 = certainly would. Return: {"ptv": <0-10>} ``` ::: ::: --- ## 3. The study's scripts, by group Before writing anything, look at what the group's own message factory wrote. The pre-registered study fields fifteen scripts: for each of three issues, four written for positions 20, 40, 60 and 80 on a left–right scale for that issue, and one **untargeted** script on a different matter altogether, the control. They were frozen with the registration, and all fifteen have already been put to all 400 twins. One caution about these answers. They were generated before the registration was finalised, with an earlier interview that asked the model to answer *as* the person, and with four questions rather than one. Only the vote-likelihood answer is used here. The block below defines the scoring used in the rest of the notebook, and prints nothing: - `group_means()` gives each ad's mean vote likelihood (0–10) in each of the five groups; - `aim()` gives each ad's **aim**: the mean in the group it was written for, minus the average of the means in the other four groups. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} read_jsonl <- function(f) { if (!file.exists(f) || length(readLines(f, warn = FALSE)) == 0) return(data.table()) rbindlist(lapply(readLines(f, warn = FALSE), function(l) as.data.table(fromJSON(l))), fill = TRUE) } group_means <- function(ans) { d <- merge(ans, panel[!is.na(group), .(twin_id, group)], by = "twin_id") d[, .(n = .N, ptv = round(mean(ptv), 2)), by = .(ad_id, group)] } aim <- function(gm, targets) { # targets: ad_id, target (a group) d <- merge(gm, targets[, .(ad_id, target)], by = "ad_id") d[, .(target_ptv = ptv[group == target[1]], others_ptv = round(mean(ptv[group != target[1]]), 2)), by = .(ad_id, target)][ , aim := round(target_ptv - others_ptv, 2)][] } ``` ::: The next block reads the cached answers and prints the five group means for the five scripts on your issue, one row per script. **Table 3.1.** `study`: mean vote likelihood by group, for the study's scripts on your issue. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} study_ads <- fread(file.path(DATA, "ads_frozen.csv"))[issue == ISSUE] study_ads[, script := ifelse(arm == "targeted", paste("position", target_position), "untargeted")] cached <- read_jsonl(file.path(DATA, "ad_answers.jsonl"))[ad_id %in% study_ads$ad_id, .(twin_id, ad_id, ptv = as.numeric(ptv))] study <- merge(group_means(cached), study_ads[, .(ad_id, script)], by = "ad_id") dcast(study, ad_id + script ~ factor(group, levels = GROUPS$group), value.var = "ptv") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|ad_id |script | SD| WD| IND| WR| SR| |:------|:-----------|----:|----:|----:|----:|----:| |IMM_20 |position 20 | 9.09| 8.41| 6.18| 3.67| 1.65| |IMM_40 |position 40 | 0.71| 1.99| 3.63| 7.71| 9.32| |IMM_60 |position 60 | 0.28| 1.19| 3.05| 7.09| 9.03| |IMM_80 |position 80 | 0.21| 0.96| 2.50| 7.28| 9.11| |IMM_U |untargeted | 7.70| 7.18| 6.37| 7.71| 8.72|
::: ::: **Figure 3.1.** The same, as five bars per script: one bar per group, strong Democrats on the left, strong Republicans on the right. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(study, aes(x = factor(group, levels = GROUPS$group), y = ptv, fill = group)) + geom_col() + facet_wrap(~ script, nrow = 1) + scale_fill_manual(NULL, values = GROUP_COLOURS, guide = "none") + scale_x_discrete(NULL) + scale_y_continuous("Mean vote likelihood, 0-10", limits = c(0, 10)) + theme_minimal() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02_silicon_voters_files/figure-html/study-plot-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: **Exercise 3.1.** Suppose you had to pick one of these five scripts to win over **weak or leaning Republicans** (`WR`). Which script has the highest mean with that group in Table 3.1? Now compute each script's **aim** for that group with `aim(study, study_ads[, .(ad_id, target = "WR")])`. Is the script with the highest bar also the script with the best aim? Why might they differ? --- ## 4. Stage 1: the basic prompt From here on a language model writes the ads. The factory is a single call to the workshop model with a prompt printed in full below: one prompt, one call, no hidden machinery. `{issue}` and `{group}` are filled in for each ad, so one prompt writes five ads, one per group. The block below reads your key and the proxy address from the environment, defines the prompts and the model calls, and prints the Stage 1 prompt. - `fill()` puts the issue and the group into a prompt; - `write_ads()` sends a filled prompt for each group and returns the five ads. The workshop model sometimes declines to write a political ad aimed at a named group of voters ("Sorry, I can't create targeted political persuasion…"); when it does, `write_ads()` asks again, up to three times, and column `asked` records how many tries each ad took. An ad still declined after three tries is marked `declined` and is not scored; - `run_ads()` puts each ad to the audience and to the judges (below). **Text 4.1.** The Stage 1 prompt. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} MODEL <- "gpt-5-mini-2025-08-07" key <- Sys.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY") base <- Sys.getenv("OPENAI_BASE_URL", unset = "https://api.openai.com/v1") API <- paste0(sub("/+$", "", base), "/chat/completions") STAGE1 <- paste( "Write the script for a thirty-second television advertisement by a candidate running for office in Ohio.", "75 to 85 words, spoken by the candidate in the first person, ending with \"And I approve this message.\"", "Name no candidate, party or office. The advertisement is about {issue}. It should win the vote of {group} in Ohio.") STAGE2_ADD <- paste( "Write it the way a real candidate speaks. Say once, flatly, what you did before politics that gives you the right", "to talk about this: a job, a service, a business. Put in one concrete scene or detail, a person, a street, a price,", "invented but with nobody named. Promise what you will do in plain verbs, naming the instrument, never \"fix\" or", "\"stand up to\". Short spoken sentences, contractions, no hedging, no balancing the other side, no neat parallel", "closing line.") EXAMPLE_ADD <- "Mention one thing the voter can check for themselves." # the worked example of Stage 3 (Section 6) fill <- function(prompt, group) paste0( gsub("{group}", GROUPS$phrase[match(group, GROUPS$group)], gsub("{issue}", it$issue, prompt, fixed = TRUE), fixed = TRUE), "\n\nReturn the script only.") chat <- function(messages, response_format = NULL) { body <- list(model = MODEL, reasoning_effort = "low", messages = messages) if (!is.null(response_format)) body$response_format <- response_format httr2::request(API) |> httr2::req_auth_bearer_token(key) |> httr2::req_body_json(body) |> httr2::req_retry(max_tries = 3) |> httr2::req_timeout(120) } perform_all <- function(reqs, workers = 8) { if (packageVersion("httr2") >= "1.1.0") httr2::req_perform_parallel(reqs, on_error = "continue", max_active = workers, progress = FALSE) else httr2::req_perform_parallel(reqs, pool = curl::new_pool(total_con = workers, host_con = workers), on_error = "continue", progress = FALSE) } content_of <- function(r) if (inherits(r, "error") || is.null(r)) NA_character_ else trimws(httr2::resp_body_json(r)$choices[[1]]$message$content) n_words <- function(x) lengths(strsplit(x, "\\s+")) is_ad <- function(x) !is.na(x) & grepl("approve this message", x, ignore.case = TRUE) & !grepl("^\\W*(sorry|i'm sorry|i am sorry|i can.?t|i cannot)", x, ignore.case = TRUE) write_ads <- function(prompt, id_prefix, tries = 3) { # asks again, up to `tries` times, for any ad the model declined text <- rep(NA_character_, nrow(GROUPS)); asked <- integer(nrow(GROUPS)) for (t in seq_len(tries)) { todo <- which(!is_ad(text)) if (!length(todo)) break reqs <- lapply(GROUPS$group[todo], function(g) chat(list(list(role = "user", content = fill(prompt, g))))) text[todo] <- vapply(perform_all(reqs), content_of, character(1)); asked[todo] <- t } data.table(ad_id = paste0(id_prefix, "_", GROUPS$group), issue = it$key, target = GROUPS$group, prompt = prompt, text = text, asked = asked, declined = !is_ad(text))[, words := n_words(text)][] } cat(strwrap(STAGE1, width = 90), sep = "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Write the script for a thirty-second television advertisement by a candidate running for office in Ohio. 75 to 85 words, spoken by the candidate in the first person, ending with "And I approve this message." Name no candidate, party or office. The advertisement is about {issue}. It should win the vote of {group} in Ohio. ``` ::: ::: ### The audience and the judges Four hundred twins is more than a live round needs. The next block draws the **audience** for every ad in Stages 1 to 3: ten twins from each group, fifty in all, with a fixed seed so that everyone in the room scores on the same fifty. It also loads the **real ads**: ten thirty-second campaign spots, nine from Ohio and one from Illinois, taken from Google's political-ad archive with the candidates' names removed (five Republican, five Democratic). They are what the judges compare each machine-written ad with. Each ad is shown to **forty judges**, separate calls to the same model, each with one real ad, and each judge is asked which of the two is the real one. Every machine-written ad meets each of the ten real ads four times: twice with the real ad shown first (text A) and twice with it shown second (text B). The order matters because the judges lean towards text A, and showing each pairing both ways means that lean weighs the same on every ad. An ad's **spotted** score is the share of its judges who picked the real ad correctly: 0.5 is what guessing gives, so an ad near 0.5 or below reads like a real one, and 1 means every judge saw through it. An ad **passes** if at least one judge was fooled. The block prints the judge's instruction, and one real ad so you can hear what the judges hear. **Text 4.2.** The judge's instruction, and one of the real ads. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(2026) audience <- panel[!is.na(group), .SD[sample(.N, 10)], by = group] real_ads <- read_jsonl(file.path(DATA, "real_ads_judges.jsonl")) N_JUDGES <- 40 JUDGE <- paste( "You are shown two texts. Each is the spoken words of a thirty-second American political advertisement.", "One of them is a real advertisement that a candidate's campaign put on the air. The other was written", "by a machine imitating one. Names have been removed from both.\nSay which one is the real advertisement.\n", "Return only: {\"real\": \"A\" or \"B\", \"confidence\": <50-100>}") JUDGE_SCHEMA <- list(type = "object", additionalProperties = FALSE, required = c("real", "confidence"), properties = list(real = list(type = "string", enum = list("A", "B")), confidence = list(type = "integer", minimum = 50, maximum = 100))) twin_request <- function(persona_text, script) chat( list(list(role = "system", content = HEADER), list(role = "user", content = paste0("=== PROFILE ===\n", persona_text, "\n=== END OF PROFILE ===\n\n", question_block(script)))), response_format = list(type = "json_schema", json_schema = list(name = "ptv", strict = TRUE, schema = SCHEMA))) judge_pairs <- function(id) { # every real ad in both slots, A and B; the same draw for the same ad, every run set.seed(sum(utf8ToInt(id) * seq_along(utf8ToInt(id)))) grid <- CJ(ref_id = real_ads$ref_id, real_pos = c("A", "B")) grid <- grid[rep(seq_len(.N), ceiling(N_JUDGES / .N))][sample(.N)][seq_len(N_JUDGES)] data.table(ad_id = id, judge = seq_len(N_JUDGES), grid) } judge_request <- function(machine, real, real_pos) chat( list(list(role = "user", content = paste0(JUDGE, "\n\nText A:\n", if (real_pos == "A") real else machine, "\n\nText B:\n", if (real_pos == "A") machine else real))), response_format = list(type = "json_schema", json_schema = list(name = "judge", strict = TRUE, schema = JUDGE_SCHEMA))) run_ads <- function(ads) { # ads: ad_id, text. 50 twins + 40 judges per ad, all in parallel tw <- CJ(ad = seq_len(nrow(ads)), k = seq_len(nrow(audience))) jp <- rbindlist(lapply(ads$ad_id, judge_pairs)) reqs <- c(lapply(seq_len(nrow(tw)), function(r) twin_request(audience$persona_text[tw$k[r]], ads$text[tw$ad[r]])), lapply(seq_len(nrow(jp)), function(r) judge_request(ads[ad_id == jp$ad_id[r], text], real_ads[ref_id == jp$ref_id[r], text], jp$real_pos[r]))) resps <- perform_all(reqs) failed <- vapply(resps, function(r) inherits(r, "error") || is.null(r), logical(1)) first_error <- if (any(failed)) conditionMessage(resps[[which(failed)[1]]]) else NA_character_ out <- vapply(resps, content_of, character(1)) t_out <- out[seq_len(nrow(tw))]; j_out <- out[nrow(tw) + seq_len(nrow(jp))] answers <- tw[, .(ad_id = ads$ad_id[ad], twin_id = audience$twin_id[k], persona_sha256 = audience$persona_sha256[k], ptv = vapply(t_out, function(x) if (is.na(x)) NA_real_ else as.numeric(fromJSON(x)$ptv), numeric(1)), model = MODEL)][!is.na(ptv)] jp[, `:=`(pick = vapply(j_out, function(x) if (is.na(x)) NA_character_ else fromJSON(x)$real, character(1)), confidence = vapply(j_out, function(x) if (is.na(x)) NA_real_ else as.numeric(fromJSON(x)$confidence), numeric(1)), model = MODEL)] jp[, spotted := pick == real_pos] list(answers = answers, judges = jp[!is.na(pick)], failed = sum(failed), first_error = first_error) } scoreboard <- function(ads, answers, judges) { a <- aim(group_means(answers), ads) s <- judges[, .(judges = .N, spotted = round(mean(spotted), 2)), by = ad_id] d <- merge(merge(ads[, .(ad_id, target)], a[, .(ad_id, target_ptv, others_ptv, aim)], by = "ad_id"), s, by = "ad_id") d[, passes := spotted < 1][order(match(target, GROUPS$group))] } five_bars <- function(ads, answers) { gm <- merge(group_means(answers), ads[, .(ad_id, target)], by = "ad_id") gm[, panel := paste("written for", GROUPS$label[match(target, GROUPS$group)])] gm[, panel := factor(panel, levels = paste("written for", GROUPS$label))] ggplot(gm, aes(x = factor(group, The black lines are 95% confidence intervals. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} spotted_bars(list(`Stage 1` = sb1, `Stage 2` = sb2), STAGE_JUDGES) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02_silicon_voters_files/figure-html/stage2-spotted-plot-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: *Note to Figure 5.2.* Each bar is a share of judge calls: of the 40 calls for one ad, or the 200 for the five pooled, the share in which the judge picked the real ad. Much of the noise in that share has a known source. Which real ad a judge saw, and whether it was shown first or second, moves the chance of a correct pick more than anything else: some real ads are picked almost every time when shown first and almost never when shown second. Every machine-written ad meets the same real ads in the same slots, so this does not favour any ad, and the intervals take it out. They come from a linear regression of each call's `spotted` (1 if the judge picked the real ad, 0 if not) on one indicator for each ad, or for each stage in the pooled bars, and one fixed effect for each pairing of real ad and slot (A or B), coded to sum to zero; because every ad meets each pairing equally often, each ad's coefficient is exactly its share. The intervals are the coefficient plus and minus 1.96 standard errors, with the residual variance pooled over all the calls in the figure, so every ad's interval has the same width. They take the ads as given: they measure how much a share would move with another set of judges for *these* ads, not the larger variation that would come from the model writing a different ad from the same prompt. Whether the Stage 2 prompt would also beat Stage 1 with five other ads is a question only more ads can answer. **Exercise 5.1.** Did the Stage 2 paragraph make the ads harder to spot, on average across the five rows of Table 5.1 and in Figure 5.2? The session now shows that loop running. Two parts of it are not in this package and are not on GitHub: the search itself — how prompts and ads are mutated and selected — and the tuning of the audience sample. The construction of the twins, the question and the scoring are all here, in the open, exactly as the group runs them. That line is drawn on purpose, and it is drawn here so that you do not have to find it. --- ## 8. What a twin cannot know Three things to carry out of the room. The twin answers from a persona built from a census cell and a matched survey respondent's own answers. It has never seen an advertisement rated by that respondent, and it was told nothing about this study. When an ad scores well, you can read the persona and see why; when it scores badly, the same. Whether the twins' ratings match those of the people they are built from is an open question, and the group is answering it the only way that counts: a pre-registered study (OSF, DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/CKAM2, 7 October 2026) in which each human respondent rates the fifteen scripts of Section 3 on four questions, and the model predicts that person's answers from their profile. Today you asked one of those questions, vote likelihood, about ads a model wrote to your instructions. Until the humans have answered, a leaderboard is a leaderboard of twins. The judges are a model too: a judge may recognise a real ad from memory, which works against you, and a human viewer may spot habits the judges miss. And a choice worth noticing: this morning's vote module asked the model to estimate *probabilities* about a record, as an analyst; this afternoon the model predicted the *answer* a particular person would give, on the scale that person sees. They are different instruments, and a method that cannot say which it used is not a method. The registered study uses the second.
